query: For refractory high-entropy alloys intended for jet-turbine applications, what single intervention could improve high-temperature mechanical capability while limiting density and preserving room-temperature performance? Formulate one hypothesis that specifies the intervention, its mechanism, the expected improvement relative to a relevant baseline, the temperature and loading conditions under which it should hold, supporting evidence from prior studies, and a decisive experiment with a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a trace amount (~0.1 at%) of carbon to a refractory high‐entropy alloy will induce the in situ formation of a fine dispersion of carbide precipitates during high-temperature exposure. This microstructural modification will increase the high-temperature yield strength by impeding dislocation motion without appreciably changing the alloy’s density or degrading its room-temperature ductility.
generation.material_initial_state: A single-phase, refractory high-entropy alloy (e.g., a Mo–Nb–Re–Ta–W based alloy) with acceptable room-temperature ductility but limited high-temperature strength.
generation.intervention: Introduce a trace carbon doping (~0.1 at%) into the alloy composition.
generation.conditions: The alloy is subjected to operational conditions typical of jet-turbine applications: tensile loading at high temperatures (approximately 800–1000 °C) while maintaining room-temperature performance.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of fine, dispersed carbide precipitates (e.g., Ta3C and/or Nb3C) that develop during high-temperature exposure.
generation.mechanism: The carbide precipitates act as obstacles to dislocation motion and grain-boundary sliding under high-temperature loading, thereby enhancing yield strength. At room temperature, the trace amount of carbon does not trigger significant phase changes or brittle intermetallic formation, preserving ductility and keeping the alloy’s density nearly unchanged.
generation.predicted_outcome: The carbon-doped alloy should exhibit an increase in high-temperature yield strength (on the order of roughly 10–25% relative to the undoped baseline) while showing similar room-temperature mechanical properties and overall density.
generation.baseline: The same refractory high-entropy alloy without carbon addition.
generation.boundary: This strengthening effect is expected only if the carbon content is carefully limited (~0.1 at%) so that carbide precipitation occurs in a fine, controlled manner. Excess carbon or different processing routes might lead to coarse or excessive carbide formation that could deteriorate room-temperature ductility.
generation.uncertainty: The precise magnitude of high-temperature strengthening and the stability of the nanoprecipitates under service conditions require experimental validation. Additionally, scalability and process reproducibility for aerospace-grade alloys remain to be established.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of refractory HEA samples with identical processing parameters: one set without carbon (baseline) and one with ~0.1 at% carbon addition. Ensure that both sets are processed to have similar grain sizes and phase distributions at room temperature. Perform tensile tests at room temperature and at high temperatures (e.g., 800–1000 °C) to assess yield strength and ductility. Microstructural characterization (using TEM or XRD) should verify the presence, size, and distribution of carbide precipitates in the carbon-doped samples.
measurements: High-temperature yield strength (e.g., via tensile testing at 800–1000 °C)
Alloy density (via rule of mixtures or direct measurement)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the carbon-doped alloy does not exhibit a statistically significant improvement (e.g., less than ~10% increase) in high-temperature yield strength compared to the undoped baseline, or if a degradation of room-temperature ductility is observed due to coarse or excessive carbide formation, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: In this work, the formation of carbide with the concertation of carbon at 0.1 at.% in refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) Mo15Nb20Re15Ta30W20 was studied under both ambient and high-pressure high-temperature conditions. The x-ray diffraction of dilute carbon (C)-doped RHEA under ambient pressure showed that the phases and lattice constant of RHEA were not influenced by the addition of 0.1 at.% C. In contrast, C-doped RHEA showed unexpected phase formation and transformation under combined high-pressure and high-temperature conditions by resistively employing the heated diamond anvil cell (DAC) technique. The new FCC_L12 phase appeared at 6 GPa and 809 °C and preserved the ambient temperature and pressure. High-pressure and high-temperature promoted the formation of carbides Ta3C and Nb3C, which are stable and may further improve the mechanical performance of the dilute C-doped alloy Mo15Nb20Re15Ta30W20.
